Application No. 243 of 1991 (Dhaka) 
Application No. 3 of 1985 (Chittagong)
lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Nihad Kabir, Advocates ----- For the Applicant
AY Salehuzzaman, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Dhamai Tea Company Ltd. care of James Finlay, Chittagong ------ Appellant
vs

full_judgment:
2. The assesse in the instant case is Dhamai Tea Company Ltd, a Company incorporated in England and admittedly the applicant was the owner of the three tea estates now situated in Bangladesh previously in East Pakistan. It is the case of the assesse that they decided to sell the tea estates and accordingly, they negotiated for sale with the purchaser in 1975. A contract for sale was ultimately executed by the applicant on 15.10.76 for sale of the said tea estates at a total consideration of Taka 52,50,000.00. The possession of the said tea estates were handed over to the purchaser on 3.1.77 in full settlement of the consideration. The aforesaid sale of the three tea estates along with their sale value was duly approved by the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Land Administration. Land, the other assets like the buildings, structures, plants, machinery, furniture, motor vehicles were sold at their written down value and it amounted in total to Taka 52,50,000.00 which included the price of plants, machinery, furniture, motor vehicles, and buildings and the land of these three tea estates. The applicant, submitted income tax return for the assessment year 1978-79 recording the sale value of the said tea estates at Taka 52,50,000.00 in its profit and loss account for the financial year ending on 31st December, 1977. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, however did not accept the above sale value of the said tea estates and by his order dated 31.5.82 fixed the consolidated sale value of the said tea estate at Taka 4,00,00,000.00 and assessed the tax on the total value of the sale proceeds at Taka 4 crore deducting most of the estates with buildings, plant machinery, etc. on the date of transfer at Taka 31,17,966.00 other expenses allowed on estimate for finalizing the sales including the agency commission to James Finlay Co &. Ltd. Total gains on the transfer of the properties was thus, estimated at Taka 3,63,82,034 the alleged income under section 10(2) (vii) of the Income Tax Act. The Deputy Commissioner however, did not follow the double taxation agreement with UK in charging 10% tax of the interest. The fixation of the consolidated amount of Taka 4,00,00,000.00 as the fair market value of the said tea estates had no legal or factual basis. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes did not consider the market value of the said tea estates prevailing at the time of negotiation and sale. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes also did not consider the financial position of the said tea estates for the period prior to the sale. The said arbitrary consolidated amount has been fixed without investigation as to the nature and condition of the said tea estates. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes has incorrectly applied the principle of Rule 38 in fixing 60:40 ratio computation of capital gain from agricultural and non-agricultural land of the said tea estates. The sale of buildings, plants, machinery and other moveables having been sold at the written down value and there cannot be any tax under section 10(2) (vii) of the Income-Tax Act and hence the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes has incorrectly assessed the tax under section 10(2) (vii) by taking the estimated sale value. Being aggrieved by the order of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, the assesse preferred an appeal before the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes and the Joint Commissioner of Taxes, however, upheld the order of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes with certain modification. Being aggrieved with the order of the said Joint Appellate Commissioner of Taxes, the assesse preferred a second appeal being Appeal No. 079 of 1983-84 before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Chittagong. The Tribunal vide its order dated 30.7.84 upheld the order of the Joint Appellate Commissioner of Taxes and rejected the objections of the applicant, against which the assesse has submitted this reference application under section 66(1) of Income Tax Act which is heard and disposed of by this judgment. 

 3. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the applicant, argued the matter from a different viewpoint which, however, is not taken in the application itself as submitted before us under section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. Mr. Syed Ishtaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel, made it short by attacking at the root of the assessment submitting that he is not questioning the assessment from the point of view of any non-consideration of the allowances out from a point of back of jurisdiction. According to him, the assessment of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes suffers from an initial infirmity because of the fact that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes was not competent to assess the capital gains before the sale, exchange or transfer of the concerned tea garden belonging to the assesse actually took place, and according to the learned Counsel, the sale actually took place in the year 1984, so the assessment year would be 1985 for the capital gains accrued in 1984 but in spite of this factual position which was before the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes committed an illegality in assessing tax on capital gains which accrued to the assesse not during the assessment year 1978-79 but assessment year 1983-84. To substantiate this argument Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submitted that there is no ambiguity in the averments which seems to be there, because in this application though it has not categorically challenged the illegality of the initial assessment, it has however been stated in this application drafted by a different lawyer in a different chamber, that in two of the applications the negotiation for sale by the purchaser began in 1975 and a contract for sale was ultimately executed by the assesse on 15.10.76 for sale of the said three tea estates at a total consideration of Taka 52,50,000.00 and the possession of the said tea estates handed over to the purchaser on 3.1.77 on full settlement of the consideration, but there is no averments in the application before the Assessment Officer that the sale actually took place during the year 1977 for the capital gain to be assessed next year namely, in 1978-79. It is the contention of learned Counsel that in the income tax return for the year 1978-79 the assesse showed no income but had submitted the sale value of the gardens on the asking of the Assessment Officer and there is no warrant for the view that the assesse themselves appeared before the Assessment Officer initially and wanted the assessment to be completed including the capital gains assessed for the year 1978-79 and he has submitted before us a copy of the tax return for the assessment year 1978-79 to which we shall advert at the relevant portion of the judgment. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, the leaned Counsel has referred to us the relevant provision of law namely, section 12B of the Income Tax Act which provided that the tax shall be payable by an assessed under the head 'Capital gains' in respect of any profit or gains arising from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset and such profits and gains shall be deemed to be income of the previous year in which the sale, exchange or transfer took place, asserting that none of the provisos to section 1211 of the Income Tax Act are referable in the instant case but only section 12B which clearly stipulated that it should be the income of the previous year in which the sale, exchange or transfer took place. There lies the illegality of the assessment and even if the assesse would have submitted to the jurisdiction of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes yet the assessment would not be made legally by submitting to a wrong jurisdiction. According to the learned Counsel, the assessment, therefore, initially was a nullity having been assessed in the year when it was not due to be assessed and, according to the learned Counsel, the assesse would have to be taxed on the capital gains as provided under section 128 of the Income Tax Act and would have to pay according to the value of the sale proceeds as decided on a proper hearing after the due enquiry by the revenue which, however, has not been done in the instant case. According to the learned Counsel, in the instant case there was no proper enquiry on the spot and no proper assessment has been made for coming to the arbitrary figure of Taka 4 crore being the total value of the capital gains or the sale proceeds which however, according to the learned Counsel, would be corrected when properly assessed by annulling the instant assessment because the present assessment was made without jurisdiction. 

 5. We find enough substance in the contention of the learned Counsel. In the instant case it appears that the Commissioner of Taxes assessed the assesse to tax on capital gain for the assessment year 1978-79 ending on 31.12.77 and that is the assessment year 1978-79. We have examined the income tax return itself, having been sent to us on our query and we find that the return has been filed showing a loss account and the column, under the head business', profession or vocation profits and, gains, share of profits of a registered firm, share of profits of an unregistered firm, is completely vacant. It has been further stated therein that the statement of accounts is attached. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed has submitted before us the statement of accounts also and from the statements of accounts we find that there it was shown a net loss for the year amounting to £ 4252 and in that statement the commission and agency fee and corporation adjustment-1976, Head office Management Expenses, Auditors Fees, terminal gratuities to garden managers has been shown as expenditure and the net loss for the year carried forward to Taka 110,519. We have examined the income tax assessment return for the same year regarding the other tea gardens and they appeared to be same. We have further seen from the supplementary reference application where certain facts had been mentioned and it is to the effect that the agreement for sale is dated 15.10.76 concerning the three tea estates. The possession of the tea estates was handed over to the purchaser on 3.1.77. The assesse first filed an application for the income tax certificate for transfer of the property as required under law to the relevant authority on 5.1.77 and the revised application for certificate of transfer of the property was filed on 12.9.78 which clearly shows that there was no complete transfer as contemplated under section 12B of the Income Tax Act for the year 1977 and we have further seen that the Appellate Joint Commissioner of Taxes also noted that there was absence of the date of sale. That being the position, it appears that the assesse did not go before the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes submitting a return showing capital gains during the assessment year 1978-79 but it only showed a net loss which return is followed by a statement of account where also it is shown to be a loss as per audited account and no mention of the capital gain to have accrued during assessment year for the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes to bring the tax for the assessment year in question. The Deputy Commissioner of Taxes would tax on capital gain as under section 12B of the Income Tax Act, 1922 and it contemplates a sale or exchange or a transfer during the assessment year. As agreement for sale having transferred no interest is to be registered compulsorily under the Registration Act nor under the Transfer of Property Act Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel, submitted that though there was an agreement for sale and delivery of possession at the beginning of the year 1977 the sale document was actually executed in the year 1984 and registered on 13th day of December, 1984. This factual aspect of the matter of sale having taken place in a particular year when the sale deed was executed and registered is a consideration of fact and material fact for a decision on the point of law as to whether an assessment as to the capital gains arises in a particular year and could be legal to be assessed in that year. It would certainly be referable to the fact as to when the sale took place. This question of fact, therefore, is not a question of fact unrelated to the question of law and both are to be considered simultaneously and the power of this court to decide so would not be questioned on the argument that the High Court under section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 acts in mere advisory capacity and not as a court of appeal. As a court of reference, the High Court jurisdiction to go into this fact of jurisdiction of assessment would be inherent in its power to decide a question of law referred to.
